young.html: Sophocles lived in Athens when it was at its height, and wrote more than a hundred plays. Seven survive. Two of the most famous are about one unlucky royal family of the city of Thebes.

In Oedipus the King, a terrible sickness has struck Thebes. King Oedipus, who once saved the city by answering the riddle of a monster called the Sphinx, promises to find out what caused it. A message from the god Apollo says: find the man who killed the old king. Oedipus is a great puzzle-solver, and he will not stop asking questions, even when people beg him to. The answer turns out to be the worst possible: he himself, without knowing it, is the man he is hunting.

In Antigone, Oedipus' daughter Antigone faces a hard choice. Her two brothers have killed each other in a war over the throne. The new king, Creon, says one brother may be buried but the other, who attacked the city, must be left unburied. Antigone believes the gods require every family to bury its dead, so she buries him anyway, and she will not say she is sorry. Is she right to break the king's law?

Solve the riddle. The old story says the Sphinx asked: What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening? Oedipus answered: a human being, who crawls as a baby, walks upright as a grown-up, and uses a cane when old. Make up a riddle of your own about something in your house, and try it on your family.

full.html: Sophocles (c. 496–406 BC) was from Colonus, just outside Athens. His long life spanned the city's golden age: he was a teenager at the time of Salamis and died two years before Athens lost the Peloponnesian War. He was elected one of the city's generals, serving with Pericles around 441 BC, and won first prize at the festival of Dionysus around 20 times, more than any other tragedian. Ancient sources say he wrote about 123 plays. Aristotle credits him with adding a third actor.

Seven plays survive: Ajax, Antigone (c. 441 BC), The Women of Trachis, Oedipus the King (also called Oedipus Tyrannus, c. 429 BC), Electra, Philoctetes (409 BC) and Oedipus at Colonus (staged after his death, in 401 BC). The three Theban plays are often read together, but they were written many years apart and are not a trilogy.

The play is built like a detective story in which the detective is also the culprit. Step by step, the prophet Tiresias, Queen Jocasta, a messenger from Corinth and an old shepherd each supply a piece. Oedipus learns that he was the baby abandoned long ago because of a prophecy, that the stranger he killed in a quarrel on the road was his father, King Laius, and that the queen he married is his mother. Jocasta dies, and Oedipus blinds himself. The chorus ends the play:

full.text: Residents of our native Thebes, behold, this is Oedipus, who knew the renowned riddle, and was a most mighty man. What citizen did not gaze on his fortune with envy? See into what a stormy sea of troubles he has come! Therefore, while our eyes wait to see the final destined day, we must call no mortal happy until he has crossed life’s border free from pain.
full.author: Sophocles
full.note: As given in the Perseus Digital Library, which prints Jebb's prose translation in lightly modernized English.

full.html: Reversal and recognition. Aristotle's Poetics holds up Oedipus as the model tragedy: the messenger who comes to cheer Oedipus brings the opposite (a reversal, peripeteia), at the very moment Oedipus learns the truth (a recognition, anagnorisis).
Antigone tells Creon why she disobeyed him:

full.text: Yes, since it was not Zeus that published me that edict, and since not of that kind are the laws which Justice who dwells with the gods below established among men. Nor did I think that your decrees were of such force, that a mortal could override the unwritten and unfailing statutes given us by the gods. For their life is not of today or yesterday, but for all time, and no man knows when they were first put forth.
full.author: Sophocles
full.note: As given in the Perseus Digital Library, which prints Jebb's prose translation in lightly modernized English.

full.html: Creon sentences her to be shut in a rock tomb. His son Haemon, who is engaged to Antigone, pleads with him; the prophet Tiresias warns him. Creon gives way too late: Antigone, Haemon and Creon's wife all die, and Creon is left alone. Earlier, the chorus sings a famous ode on human cleverness, which can master sea and land but not death:

full.text: Wonders are many, and none is more wonderful than man.
full.author: Sophocles
full.note: As given in the Perseus Digital Library, which prints Jebb's prose translation in lightly modernized English.

full.html: Antigone has been read as the first great drama about conscience against the state: a law made by a ruler set against a law the person believes is higher. It is also a play about stubbornness on both sides, which is why readers still disagree about it.

Reading Oedipus as a man who was simply punished for a sin. The play never says the gods made him a bad man. He acts in ignorance, and his great strengths, his intelligence and his refusal to stop asking, are what bring the truth out.

deep.html: Was Oedipus free? The prophecy came true, but every step he took toward it he chose: to leave Corinth, to fight on the road, to accept the throne, to keep investigating. Ancient and modern readers have argued over how fate and choice fit together in the play. It does not settle the question; it makes the audience feel it.

The philosopher G. W. F. Hegel, in the early 1800s, read Antigone as a clash between two real goods, duty to family and the gods on one side and the order of the city on the other, each pushed too far. Others see Antigone as plainly right and Creon as plainly wrong. Both readings have long histories.

items: Is it ever right to break a law? How would you decide?
Antigone cites "unwritten laws". Are there laws no ruler can change?
Oedipus would not stop searching for the truth. Is it always better to know?
Why might the chorus say no one should be called happy until the end of their life?

deep.html: Herodotus, on a later rung, tells the same idea through the wise Athenian Solon and the rich king Croesus. Aristotle's Poetics and Plato's dialogues return again and again to these plays. The idea of an unwritten higher law runs on to Cicero, Aquinas and the natural-law thinkers later on this ladder.

questions: Oedipus keeps asking questions even when others beg him to stop. When is it good to keep digging for the truth, and when is it not?
Antigone breaks the king's law to do what she thinks is right. Was she right? What would you have done?
Creon changes his mind, but too late. What makes it hard for people in charge to admit they were wrong?
"Wonders are many, and none is more wonderful than man." What human inventions do you find most wonderful?
Why do people still enjoy plays and stories that end sadly?
care: Oedipus the King turns on a terrible discovery: without knowing it, Oedipus killed his father and married his mother. Jocasta's death and Oedipus' blinding happen offstage. Summarize these simply for young readers; Antigone's choice and the riddle of the Sphinx are the best starting points.
